transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-12-11
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 73 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Torres (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ravi Kapoor (Helix Head of ML Infra), Sara Ng (Platform Eng), Diego Morales (SRE), Anya Petrov (ML Eng)

Auto-generated Summary (may be partial):
Redwood walked through priority queue designs and prewarm patterns to keep Helix latency under 120ms p95 during spikes. Discussed K-V cache priming, multipool reserved capacity with burst absorbers, and cost tradeoffs of more aggressive quantization. Next: share sizing scenarios and run bench on Dedicated.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, uh we thought we'd do a quick walkthrough of what a priority-based burst policy looks like on Redwood, and then dive into your specific traffic patterns. Ravi, do you wanna kick off with the workload shape?
[00:12] Ravi Kapoor: Yeah, sure, thanks. So our primary inference path is a text-generation endpoint used by a customer-facing assistant. Normal load is around 120 rps, but we see spiky bursts to 1.6k rps for short periods — like 30 to 90 seconds — usually around batch job windows. The hard SLA is 200ms p95, ideally 120ms.
[00:36] Sara Ng: And to add, we have two model sizes in prod, a medium 7B and a large 13B that we use for longer contexts. The 13B is more expensive and we want to keep it reserved for certain prioritized tenants.
[00:52] Maya Chen: Understood. One clarifying Q: are those spikes simultaneous across regions or mostly single-region?
[00:58] Ravi Kapoor: Mostly single-region, US-east, but sometimes multi-region when a release toggles a feature flag.
[01:06] Liam Torres: Cool. So the main levers we'll look at: (1) priority queueing with capacity bands, (2) prewarmed reserved pools + burst absorbers, and (3) KV cache warmups and continuous caching to reduce per-token compute. We'll also talk about batch sizing to balance throughput vs tail latency.
[01:25] Diego Morales: When you say prewarmed pools, do you mean we buy reserved GPUs and keep them warm? We're worried about cost if they sit idle.
[01:32] Priya Nair: Right, there's a playbook. You can have multipool: a small steady-state reserved pool sized for baseline (120 rps), a prewarmed burst pool that's mostly idle but has KV caches primed, and an on-demand burst absorber that can spin up ephemeral instances or use burst credits. The idea is to tune the prewarm so the first few tokens hit a hot KV cache and reduce cold-starts.
[01:54] Ravi Kapoor: How do you prime the K-V cache without paying compute for warm workers?
[02:00] Liam Torres: Two approaches we recommend: (A) passive warmup — continuously keep a tiny number of prewarmed workers doing lightweight probes across your common prefixes, or (B) active playback — ingest a short recent traffic trace and replay prefix tokens to fill KV. Passive is low-cost but slower; playback is fast but requires a short compute window.
[02:19] Anya Petrov: Playback sounds good but is it safe for private deployments? We have PII and need to keep traces inside VPC.
[02:26] Maya Chen: Yep — for Redwood Private we can do local playback inside your VPC, Redwood only stores playback recipes not raw payloads. For Dedicated we can run a bench job in your account or in our dedicated pool per your security needs.
[02:39] Sara Ng: Ok I want to talk through the queueing model. If we do strict priority, are we going to starve lower-priority traffic? We have background analytics calls that are latency-insensitive but still need throughput.
[02:50] Liam Torres: Good point. Strict priority can starve. We usually recommend a hybrid: weighted priority or leaky-bucket per-class with a small guaranteed slice for low-priority work. Example: give p90 of resources to priority class but reserve 10% for background pool, and enforce max queue wait times with circuit-breakers that reroute to quantized variants or fallback models.
[03:12] Diego Morales: Can you show numbers? Like if baseline is 120 rps and we spike to 1600, how does p95 move?
[03:18] Liam Torres: Absolutely, we did a quick back-of-envelope earlier. For a single GPU serving 13B quantized at 4-bit with moderate batching, you might see steady throughput of X tokens/sec — sorry the number varies — but the important part is the queuing delay. If you have 10 prewarmed workers with hot KV, your tail latency stays ~150ms for priority class during 1k rps bursts because those requests hit cached KV states and batching is efficient. Lower-priority tasks will see queues and eventual fallback.
[03:46] Ravi Kapoor: What about using heavier quantization for burst tasks to fit more concurrent in a GPU? We tested int8 and saw weird hallucination rates.
[03:55] Priya Nair: Quantization tradeoffs are workload dependent. For generative assistants, int8 or 4-bit can be okay for short responses but can degrade long-form coherency. We suggest an A/B with post-hoc eval on your prompt suite. Also, Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per model segment (e.g., attention layers quantize more aggressively than embedding tables).
[04:16] Anya Petrov: Are those recommendations automated or manual?
[04:20] Liam Torres: Both. We auto-propose profiles from historical perf and fidelity, then you can approve a rollout with canary traffic and regression alerts.
[04:27] Maya Chen: Back to prewarm sizing: Diego, do you have cache hit ratios or prefix distributions?
[04:33] Diego Morales: Our KV hit is around 11% avg, but for top 200 prefixes it's 62%. We can share the distribution.
[04:41] Maya Chen: Perfect, that suggests targeted prewarm of the top 200 prefixes will get you most of the benefit at small cost.
[04:47] Sara Ng: For the multipool approach, how do we handle eviction when the burst pool fills? Is there a graceful degradation path?
[04:54] Priya Nair: Yes — eviction policy is configurable. For example: 1) reject-low-priority, 2) degrade-by-quantize (route to int8 variant), 3) route-to-fallback-model with shorter context, or 4) shed non-critical traffic to an async queue. You can combine them. We typically recommend degrade-by-quantize for short latencies, and reject for large-batch analytics.
[05:15] Ravi Kapoor: We have a VPC egress cap per month and strict peering limits. Would bursting to Redwood Dedicated in a different region hit those caps?
[05:24] Maya Chen: If you deploy Redwood Private or Dedicated within your cloud account, traffic stays within your VPC and egress counts are per-region per-account. For Hosted, we can route via private endpoints and maintain egress maps but yes, cross-region bursts could increase egress. We can add region affinity and prefer local region burst absorbers.
[05:41] Anya Petrov: I want to understand practical numbers for reserved GPU sizing. What's the rule of thumb?
[05:46] Liam Torres: A simple heuristic: size reserved GPUs for 1.5x your baseline RPS converted to tokens/sec for your largest model. Example: baseline 120 rps with 150 tokens avg per request at 13B => 18k tokens/sec. If each GPU does 6k tokens/sec at your quantization/profile, you'd need 3 GPUs reserved (18k/6k). Then add prewarm and burst pools to hit 1.6k spike. But we always validate with a bench run because kernel selection and sequence length distribution matter a lot.
[06:18] Diego Morales: How much do KV caches reduce the tokens/sec pressure?
[06:22] Priya Nair: If the prefix is served from KV, you skip re-computing previous layers and only do delta tokens. That can reduce per-request compute by 30-60% for long-context assistants. For short prompts it helps less.
[06:35] Sara Ng: You mentioned bench runs. What's included in that run and how long does it take?
[06:39] Maya Chen: We'll run a 2-hour bench that replays a 1-2 hour trace plus synthetic spikes. It includes quantized variants, KV warm vs cold scenarios, and mixed-priority traffic to measure p50/p95/p99. Bench results include cost estimates and recommended pool counts.
[06:55] Ravi Kapoor: For Private deployment, can the bench job run in our VPC so logs and traces never leave?
[06:59] Priya Nair: Yes, for Redwood Private or Dedicated on customer account we run bench in your environment and produce an encrypted artifact you can store. For Hosted we use anonymized traces unless you opt-in for private bench.
[07:12] Anya Petrov: A quick question on batching: we noticed increasing batch size helps throughput but makes p95 worse during spikes. Any heuristics?
[07:20] Liam Torres: Right — dynamic batching is key. Use small max batch sizes for low-latency classes and larger for background work. Redwood supports continuous batching with per-route batch caps and timeout knobs. Our rule: latency-sensitive route: max batch 8-16, timeout 8-12ms; background: 64-128, timeout 40-100ms. Also set a separate batching profile for prewarm workers to prefer single-request work to keep KV hot.
[07:46] Diego Morales: What about backpressure to upstream? Should we spike throttle at the gateway?
[07:50] Priya Nair: Yes, we recommend backpressure at the edge with token buckets per-tenant + circuit-breakers. If the queue length exceeds a threshold we return 429 for non-priority or route to degraded variant. This reduces tail latency for priority traffic.
[08:03] Ravi Kapoor: Are there observability hooks to know when KV is stale or when prewarm failed?
[08:07] Liam Torres: Absolutely — in the Redwood Console you'll get per-model KV hit ratio, per-pool utilization, and per-route latency heatmaps. We also emit traces for prewarm tasks and an alert if prewarm success rate drops below X% in a window.
[08:21] Maya Chen: Quick pause — any security or compliance blockers we should note for Private?
[08:25] Sara Ng: We'll need SOC2 Type 2 proof for Hosted and a KMS integration for key management. Also audit logs for who triggered playback.
[08:34] Maya Chen: Got it. Redwood has SOC 2 and can integrate customer-managed KMS for Private/Dedicated. Playback triggers and bench runs can be audited. We'll link the compliance deck.
[08:43] Anya Petrov: On fallback models, what does rollback look like if quality regresses due to quantization?
[08:49] Priya Nair: Rollbacks are via model version pinning and automatic canary. We run prompt suite evals during rollout; if any regresses beyond your threshold we auto-fallback to previous version. You can also set a policy to only allow quantized variants for X% of traffic or only for priority traffic.
[09:04] Ravi Kapoor: I want to talk about cost math. If we reserve 3 GPUs and add 2 prewarm nodes and occasional burst ephemeral, what's the rough monthly delta?
[09:13] Maya Chen: We'll calculate exacts in the sizing doc, but high level: reserved capacity is cheaper on committed terms; prewarm nodes are low instance-hour because they're few but continuous; burst ephemeral are pay-as-you-go. The bench run will return per-request cost at different SLOs so you can pick the cost-latency sweet spot.
[09:31] Diego Morales: Any gotchas with private peering and routing that we should plan for?
[09:35] Liam Torres: Watch MTU and TCP settings for large responses, and set up health checks on the prewarm pool. Also avoid cross-region fallbacks unless you have bandwidth — that can blow egress budgets.
[09:48] Sara Ng: Let's map next steps — Diego will share traces, Redwood sends the sizing scenarios and bench plan, then we schedule the bench.
[09:56] Maya Chen: Yep. I'll own the sizing doc. Liam will own the priority-queue config examples. Priya will attach the compliance checklist.
[10:04] Ravi Kapoor: One last thing — we have a question internally about eviction: when a burst pool evicts a worker, does its KV state get redistributed or lost?
[10:12] Priya Nair: KV state is ephemeral to the worker. If a worker is evicted we try to drain and snapshot hot prefixes to a shared store if configured, but that has tradeoffs. Usually we prefer graceful drain during eviction windows and keep the smallest number of hot workers to minimize re-warm cost. We'll show examples in the doc.
[10:29] Anya Petrov: Ok thanks, this was super helpful.
[10:32] Maya Chen: Great. We'll follow up with the artifacts. Anything else before we close?
[10:36] Ravi Kapoor: Nope, thanks all.

End of meeting.
